sentences.text: Deinocheirus stands as the largest known ornithomimosaur, with the biggest specimen estimated to reach 11 meters in length and weigh 6.36 tons.
The only known skull measures 1.024 meters in length from the premaxilla to the occipital condyle.
This animal and Therizinosaurus share the distinction of having the longest forelimbs of any known bipedal dinosaurs.
Its vertebrae featured an interconnected ligament system that stiffened the spine to support the abdomen while transferring stress to the hips and hind limbs.
Paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz described the skeleton as resembling a hybrid between a hadrosaur and Gallimimus.
The holotype specimen displayed abnormal pits, grooves, and tubercles on finger phalanges, possibly resulting from joint injuries.
The first remains were discovered in 1965 in the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia by Polish paleontologist Zofia Kielan-Jaworowska on July 9.
Two new specimens were announced in 2013 at the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology conference.
Deinocheirus likely had a specialized diet different from other ornithomimosaurs, with evidence including fish scales near a specimen and gastroliths in the stomach region.
Its blunt, short claws resemble those of the therizinosaur Alxasaurus, suggesting the long arms were used for digging and gathering plants.
The skull shape indicates a plant diet, but the animal had a weak bite force due to small muscle attachment sites relative to skull size.
A fan of feathers likely covered the tail, which ended in at least two fused vertebrae similar to the pygostyles of oviraptorosaurian and therizinosaurian theropods.
Deinocheirus is classified as a primitive ornithomimosaurian closely related to Garudimimus and Beishanlong, forming the family Deinocheiridae.
A 2014 cladogram suggested ornithomimosaurians split into Deinocheiridae and Ornithomimidae lineages in the Early Cretaceous, based on research by Barsbold et al.
Osmólska and Roniewicz created the new family Deinocheiridae within Carnosauria because they believed Deinocheirus did not fit existing theropod families.
Deinocheirus lived during the Late Cretaceous approximately 70 million years ago, specifically between 71 and 69 million years ago during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages.
The river habitats where it lived supported a wide variety of other organisms including fish, turtles, and birds.
Researchers tested geochemical methods to identify poached Deinocheirus fossils because proving provenance became a scientific and political concern.
Researchers suggest deinocheirids either originated in Laurasia or dispersed across Northern Hemisphere polar regions, similar to other Asian-affinity dinosaur groups.
The function of pneumatization in Deinocheirus is debated, with hypotheses including bone mass reduction, high metabolism, locomotion balance, or thermoregulation.
Researchers suspect Deinocheirus may have reverted to an omnivorous or carnivorous diet.
